entities.summary:
David Beaton (c. 1494–1546), Archbishop of St Andrews and the last Scottish cardinal before the Reformation, was a pivotal figure in early 16th-century Scotland, fiercely defending Catholic orthodoxy against the rising tide of Protestantism. As a statesman, diplomat, and ecclesiastical leader, Beaton wielded immense political power during the tumultuous minority of Mary, Queen of Scots, aligning Scotland with France through the 'Auld Alliance' and navigating complex relations with England under Henry VIII. His uncompromising stance against heresy and his execution of Protestant reformers like George Wishart made him a symbol of the old order, directly precipitating the violent backlash that would ignite the Scottish Reformation.

Educated at the Universities of St Andrews and Glasgow, and later in Paris, Beaton’s early career saw him serve as Scotland's Resident Ambassador to France in 1519 and later as Commendator of Arbroath Abbey in 1523, accumulating significant ecclesiastical wealth and influence. He became Lord Privy Seal in 1528 and was elevated to Cardinal by Pope Paul III in 1538, a testament to his diplomatic prowess and staunch Catholicism. His political machinations included thwarting English attempts to secure a marriage alliance between Edward VI and Mary, Queen of Scots, instead negotiating Mary's eventual marriage to the French Dauphin, Francis. Between 1539 and 1546, Beaton orchestrated the trials and executions of several prominent Protestants, including the burning of Patrick Hamilton in 1528 and George Wishart in March 1546, solidifying his reputation as a persecutor of reformers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: David Beaton's fierce opposition to Protestantism and his violent death were pivotal in accelerating the Scottish Reformation, profoundly altering Scotland's religious and political landscape for centuries. His actions directly contributed to the rise of John Knox and the establishment of Presbyterianism.
